doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Ellington years, Pearl Bailey and Jazz at the Philharmonic
title: A Drum Is a Woman, Sam Woodyard and later Ellington projects
summary: Bellson says Sam Woodyard played most of A Drum Is a Woman, while he did My People and returned for the Sacred Concert.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Let’s take a little break here, because we’re getting up onto A Drum is a Woman, which is real important.
The next hallmark in your career, or at least one of the ones in the mid-’50s, would have been the recording of Duke Ellington’s magnum opus, A Drum is a Woman.
Did they give me credit for doing that? Because most of that, Sam Woodyard did – most of that. I did My People.
So that would have been the ’60s.
And then Sacred Concert as well.
The first Sacred Concert was in the ’60s.
So after you left Ellington in early ’53, that was pretty much it until you came back to do those particular projects?

Okay. So then in the mid-’50s – they’ll have to correct this one. We’ll send them a message that they need to correct this. They have you listed as recording A Drum is a Woman. I do Sam on that, but I didn’t know if you had participated as well.
I think I did a very little bit of A Drum is a Woman. I don’t know whether they give me credit. But I know Sam did most of it, Sam Woodyard.
There’s another example of Duke Ellington reversing it: jazz – zajj. That’s another one of those.
